tldr: An AI system using the Hopper algorithm generates novel polytopes with extremal properties, producing new counterexamples and bounds on three classical geometry problems, including the Hirsch conjecture.
contributions: Introduction of the Hopper algorithm, an AI-guided multi-agent approach for generating polytopes with specific extremal structures
Generation of over a million new 5-dimensional prismatoids with width 6, finding the smallest known counterexample to the Hirsch conjecture (24 vertices, dimension 19)
New bounds for the longest monotone path problem and discovery of previously unknown neighbourly polytopes that are not cyclic
Demonstration that AI-generated polytopes are fundamentally different from human-constructed ones
methods: The system uses a population of AI agents operating via a work-stealing strategy on a shared repository of polytope examples. Each agent uses the Hopper algorithm: it computes hyperplanes through subsets of vertices, feeds them through a transformer-based neural network (the 'brain') that predicts the likelihood of each hyperplane being part of a successful 'hop region', samples constraints to form a region, inscribes the largest ball within it, and 'hops' vertices to the center to generate candidate polytopes. Agents optimize fitness functions (continuous approximations of target properties), with multi-objective optimization across up to 10 fitness functions to avoid local minima. The neural network is trained online from agent experience.
results: For the Hirsch conjecture: found the smallest counterexample with 24 vertices in dimension 19 (beating the previous 25-vertex bound), with only 12 points in each base facet and width 6. None of 100 sampled AI-generated polytopes could be explained by the bipartite directed graph criterion that accounts for all human constructions. For the longest monotone path problem: achieved f(9,5)=30 (tight bound), improved lower bounds for (10,5) to 41, (11,5) to 55, and achieved f(9,6)=29 (tight). For neighbourly polytopes: found many previously unknown non-cyclic neighbourly polytopes for (n,d) pairs from (10,6) to (13,8).
limitations: Naive addition and subtraction of vertices leads to degenerate behavior (polytopes collapsing to simplices or growing indefinitely), requiring custom heuristics (uptick/downtick rules). Many pre-selection procedures rely on float representations rather than exact arithmetic. The approach requires careful selection of fitness functions, though multi-objective optimization helps navigate this.
